biography.text: Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī was a ninth-century philosopher and scholar whose writings covered mathematics, science, and philosophy. Peter Adamson's Stanford Encyclopedia account places his life approximately around 800–870 CE and describes his role in the Baghdad translation milieu. This focused dossier concerns one work attributed to him; it is not a complete biography.
gaps: Reconcile the differing death-date traditions and complete the biography from Arabic biographical sources and specialist studies.

timeline.text: The cryptanalysis treatise is assigned to al-Kindī's ninth-century milieu, but the sources consulted do not establish an exact composition year. The modern date of an edition and the date of a surviving manuscript image must not be substituted for composition date.
gaps: Establish the treatise's manuscript witness, copy date, and composition-date argument from the critical edition and catalogue records.

fields.text: Ismāʿīl Durmuş's TDV encyclopedia entry describes al-Kindī's *Risāla fī istikhrāj al-muʿammā* as distinguishing substitution and transposition, including their combination, and discussing frequency ranks alongside letter combinations and likely conventional openings. This is a secondary account of a medieval text. It supports a bounded description of a multi-clue procedure, not the claim that every cipher can be solved, that he invented all cryptography, or that the work is equivalent to modern statistical cryptanalysis.
gaps: Read the Arabic critical text and its apparatus directly, especially edition volume I, pp. 213–259; transcribe and translate a bounded passage with page-level locators.
Determine which examples and limitations belong to al-Kindī's text versus editorial headings, notes, or later summaries.

legacy.text: TDV identifies al-Kindī's treatise as the earliest surviving work on message concealment and recovery it discusses, while also reporting an earlier *Kitāb al-Muʿammā* attributed to al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad. The defensible claim is therefore about the earliest surviving treatise identified by this reference, not an absolute invention priority or proof that no earlier practice existed.
gaps: Review TDV's bibliography and the critical edition's evidence for earlier cryptological writing; trace later Arabic treatises without presuming direct borrowing.

works.subject: Methods for classifying and recovering concealed writing
works.purpose: The title and introductory description concern methods for recovering meanings from writing made obscure by unfamiliar signs. The work's detailed context and addressee require direct collation.
works.date: Associated with al-Kindī's ninth-century milieu; exact composition date not established by sources consulted here.

investigations.title: A multi-clue method in al-Kindī's treatise on concealed writing
investigations.historicalProblem: What method components does a specialist reference attribute to al-Kindī's surviving treatise, and how far can those claims be taken before the Arabic text is directly collated?
investigations.historicalContext: The Arabic reference distinguishes technical message concealment and recovery from literary riddles. It reports older writing about concealment and an earlier book attributed to al-Khalīl, then identifies al-Kindī's treatise as the earliest surviving work in its account. This dossier records those claims as a modern source's description, not a settled universal priority claim.
investigations.method: Read İsmail Durmuş's Turkish TDV entry, especially the al-Kindī discussion and bibliography (online paragraphs 121–124; print vol. 30, pp. 319–320). Use its citations to locate the 1987 edition, vol. I, pp. 213–259, and record that edition as not yet consulted. Peter Adamson's SEP article was read only for the scholar's general context, not for the cryptanalysis method. No operational demonstration or new translation was attempted.
investigations.observationsOrCalculations: The TDV account names multiple analytical cues: classification of substitution and transposition (including a combined form), ranking letters by frequency in Arabic, checking letter combinations, and considering conventional openings of letters or speeches. The dossier does not add a modern frequency table, a plaintext example, sample-size threshold, or claim that these cues guarantee recovery.
investigations.reportedResult: The sources support a bounded account that the treatise, as summarized by TDV, sets out a multi-clue approach to concealed writing. The 1987 critical edition provides a specific path for future verification, but its Arabic text has not yet been directly checked here.
investigations.whatWasNew: No claim of invention of cryptography, absolute world priority, earliest statistical inference, universal solvability, or direct European transmission is made. TDV's narrower characterization is 'the first surviving work' in the field it describes; it also reports an earlier work attributed to al-Khalīl.
investigations.limitations: The primary Arabic edition and apparatus have not been read in this batch. Method details are a Turkish reference-work summary, not a fresh translation of the treatise. The modern labels 'frequency analysis' and 'cryptanalysis' may not map exactly to the author's terms. The manuscript witness, composition date, editorial interventions, examples, and textual variants remain unverified.
investigations.laterInfluence: Not assessed. TDV lists later Arabic works, but a list does not establish direct borrowing or a transmission chain from al-Kindī to any particular author.

claims.text: Peter Adamson's SEP account identifies Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī as a ninth-century philosopher and gives approximate dates of ca. 800–870 CE.
claims.uncertainty: The dates are approximate; other reference traditions give different death dates.

claims.text: Adamson describes al-Kindī as overseeing one of two major ninth-century translator groups and as mediating between patrons and translators.
claims.uncertainty: This is a modern scholarly synthesis; translator-by-translator relationships require separate primary and specialist evidence.
